Such continuity favours relationships of trust when commitments are honoured, but may also sustain ancient disputes. A merchant may recall a debt incurred by his current partner's grandfather, while a community leader remembers the circumstances of a territorial quarrel whose consequences are still felt. The Umli therefore attach great importance to the accounts and testimony of their elders, particularly when these help explain the origin of the rights and obligations binding several families together.

Their long lives also encourage thorough apprenticeships. A master craftsman may devote several decades to perfecting his techniques, then pass on his knowledge to several generations of pupils. An experienced hunter may recognise changes in animal migrations over a period that his human companions would regard as exceptionally long, while a guide remembers paths rendered impassable after a severe winter. Such knowledge possesses collective value, enabling communities to recognise changes in their environment and adapt their activities accordingly. The death of an elder may therefore mean the loss of information accumulated over more than a century, particularly when that knowledge has neither been passed on nor recorded.

This continuity may nevertheless make certain decisions difficult. An ageing leader may remain deeply attached to a settlement threatened by changes in the climate, while a craftsman refuses to abandon a method he has employed for many decades. Younger Umli may wish to develop new commercial relationships, seek resources in distant territories, or adopt techniques learned from foreign peoples. Such plans are not always welcomed by their elders, particularly when they seem to challenge customs that have long ensured the safety of families. Generational differences thus offer important possibilities for roleplaying, without imposing excessive caution upon the old or a necessarily adventurous temperament upon the young.

Family, Tali, and Umlati

Umli society rests upon closely organised kinship relationships, whose forms have been developed in the traditions of The Northern Wastes. Marriage is traditionally monogamous, while descent is chiefly traced through the male line. Genealogies make it possible to recognise relationships between families, determine certain rights of inheritance, and preserve the memory of obligations binding several generations. These traditions do not mean that all family decisions are made by men, for everyday responsibilities depend largely upon the abilities, experience, and position of each member of the community. A woman may direct an enterprise, organise the stores, or lead an expedition when her experience makes her particularly suited to the task, while an elder retains considerable authority in matters concerning the memories and commitments of his kindred.

The Umli distinguish two principal forms of grouping: the lat, whose plural is tali, and the umlat, whose plural is umlati. The lat brings together members of a kindred whose relationships may be traced through several generations. It provides the setting in which names, memories, possessions, and certain family obligations are passed down. Its members may live in different settlements, particularly when migrations, marriages, or professional activities have caused several branches to separate. Gatherings between relatives then allow relationships to be maintained, inheritances discussed, and commitments made in the name of their lineage to be recalled. An individual may receive assistance from distant members of his lat when undertaking a journey or seeking an apprenticeship unavailable in his home settlement.

The umlat answers a different need, bringing together families sharing the same territory or a particular environment. It may include several tali whose members possess no close kinship but live and work within a common region. This organisation makes it possible to combine the abilities of different groups, particularly when a settlement includes hunters, miners, craftsmen, and people responsible for commercial exchanges. Families contribute to collective activities according to their resources and knowledge, while decisions concerning stores, passages, and the defence of dwellings involve all the inhabitants. An Umit may therefore belong to a lat whose members live in several regions and to an umlat bringing together the families established around his present home, retaining obligations towards both groups.

These affiliations may become particularly important when a community must make a difficult decision. Opening a new mine, relocating a settlement, or concluding a commercial agreement may concern several families whose interests differ. Representatives of the tali recall the rights and commitments of their kindreds, while those responsible for the umlat consider the needs of the territory and the available resources. Discussions may be lengthy, especially when elders preserve different memories of an agreement or several families believe that a decision will affect their activities. Once a commitment has been made, the Umli generally strive to honour it, for its continuity contributes to the stability of relationships upon which the security of the community often depends.

Authority nevertheless remains adapted to circumstances. An elder may preside over discussions concerning family traditions, while an experienced guide leads an expedition into the mountains. A master smith organises the work of his apprentices, and a keeper of the stores determines the quantities needed to sustain the families through winter. The same individual may fulfil several of these responsibilities during his lifetime, particularly in small settlements where available skills remain limited. Umli organisation thus values experience and the ability to perform a useful function, without excluding personal rivalries or disagreements concerning authority. A leader may be respected for prudence and knowledge, while another retains his position chiefly through the prestige of his family, giving rise to tensions when his decisions jeopardise common interests.

Growing Up and Learning in the Far North

Umli childhood generally unfolds within an extended family circle, where parents, relatives, and elders gradually contribute to the education of the young. Children first learn to recognise the places within their dwelling, the people from whom they may seek help, and the particular dangers of their surroundings. The proximity of hearths, workshops, and stores allows them to observe daily activities, while adults gradually entrust them with small tasks suited to their abilities. They may begin by putting away tools, preparing food, helping repair clothing, or watching over provisions, before taking part in more demanding work. These activities teach them the value of resources, particularly when a piece of leather, a handful of salt, or a damaged tool represents something difficult to replace during winter.

As they grow older, children discover the techniques required for travel in cold regions. They learn to recognise the quality of snow, distinguish dangerous frozen surfaces, and prepare clothing suited to long excursions. The youngest accompany adults along familiar routes, then gradually take part in longer expeditions as their experience permits. They observe animal tracks, discover shelters used during storms, and learn the precautions essential when crossing frozen rivers. Knowledge of the territory is thus transmitted through practice, during repeated journeys that allow their teachers to point out directly the signs of approaching danger. A child may recognise the path leading to a nearby hunting ground at an early age without yet knowing how to cross the distant regions travelled by experienced guides.

Craft trades require a different apprenticeship. A young Umit may be entrusted to a master smith, from whom he learns the properties of metals, the maintenance of tools, and the precautions necessary when working with furnaces. Another learns to prepare hides, cut garments, and reinforce seams intended to withstand long periods of use. Children raised in mining communities gradually discover galleries, supports, and the methods employed to identify ores, while those in riverside settlements take a greater part in fishing and maintaining equipment. Such training may continue over several years, particularly when an activity presents considerable danger or demands great precision. A master's reputation then depends as much upon the quality of his work as upon his ability to pass on knowledge to pupils who must one day practise their craft without his assistance.

Personal dispositions contribute to the choice of training. A child from a family of hunters may display particular talent for metalworking, while another, raised among craftsmen, shows greater interest in languages and commercial relations. Families may encourage these vocations when they answer the needs of the community, but may also wish to preserve the continuity of a trade or an ancient commitment. A young Umit may therefore struggle to gain acceptance for his desire to leave a family workshop, particularly when his father or grandfather believes that several generations have devoted their lives to its prosperity. Such tensions provide possible motivations for a character, whose departure may arise as much from personal ambition as from necessity imposed by circumstances.

The Seasons and Mastery of the Land

The lives of the Umli closely follow the rhythm of the seasons, animal migrations, and available resources. During winter, communities remain closer to their protected settlements, particularly when storms make travel dangerous. Work then centres upon maintaining tools, repairing clothing, preparing hides, and pursuing activities that can be carried out under shelter. Forges and workshops remain active when fuel supplies permit, while families prepare the equipment required for future expeditions. Excursions nevertheless remain necessary, particularly to watch the passages frequented by animals, seek certain fishing grounds, or inspect the condition of distant shelters. Every journey demands suitable preparation, for an error in choosing a route may prevent a traveller from returning before the weather suddenly deteriorates.

The Umli pay close attention to changes in the weather. Wind direction, the shape of clouds, the consistency of snow, and the movements of animals provide information upon which the safety of an expedition may depend. An experienced guide recognises signs announcing a storm, while a hunter knows how to distinguish fresh tracks from those partly erased by the wind. These observations allow them to choose favourable times for travel and determine passages where the risks remain acceptable. Strangers crossing the Far North without knowledge of these signs may make serious mistakes, particularly if they assume that ground easily crossed in summer will remain passable during the coldest months. The reputation of an Umli guide therefore rests upon the ability to understand circumstances and make prudent decisions, even when the travellers in his care wish to continue.

With the return of milder temperatures, families organise longer expeditions. Some travel to seasonal fishing grounds, while others follow herds or reach regions where edible plants become accessible. Skiing and skating make movement across snow and frozen surfaces easier, while sledges allow provisions, hides, and materials to be carried over long distances. Ropes are used to secure difficult passages, overcome certain obstacles, and keep loads stable when the terrain becomes uneven. Techniques vary between regions, particularly when the depth of snow, the relief, or the frequency of waterways requires different equipment. Craftsmen play an important part in its maintenance, for a broken fastening or damaged sledge may jeopardise the return of an entire expedition.

Hunting provides a considerable share of the resources required for subsistence. Meat is eaten, dried, or smoked, while fats are preserved and hides become clothing, blankets, or equipment. Bones and sinews are employed in making tools and household objects, particularly when available materials must be used with as little waste as possible. Fishing supplements this diet, notably in communities with regular access to rivers and lakes. Fish may be eaten fresh, preserved by freezing, or dried to form stores needed for the following months. Gathering supplies roots, berries, and various plants whose collection requires precise knowledge of the seasons in which they are available.

The use of these resources remains closely linked to communal customs. Families must know how much can be taken without jeopardising future expeditions, particularly when herds follow variable routes or fishing becomes less plentiful. Elders preserve memories of seasons when particular resources were scarce and recall the precautions that enabled their community to overcome those difficulties. A hunter may wish to pursue a group of animals into a distant valley, while the keeper of the stores advises him to conserve his strength for a safer expedition. Such differences of judgement may provoke discussion, but they demonstrate the importance attached to collective decisions in an environment where a reckless undertaking may affect the subsistence of several families.

Provisions, Meals, and Hospitality

Preserving food is an essential concern in Umli dwellings. Families prepare their stores during favourable seasons, then distribute them among spaces suited to different kinds of provisions. Meat is dried or smoked, fish prepared to withstand long periods of storage, and fats kept in suitable containers. Supplies of salt hold considerable importance, particularly when they improve food preservation and allow certain goods to be prepared for exchange. Those responsible for provisions must know the quantities available, the needs of the inhabitants, and the periods during which expeditions are likely to be interrupted. This organisation demands constant attention, for a mistake made before winter may have far more serious consequences than a poor decision during the warmer season.

Meals are adapted to the exertion and temperatures to which the Umli are exposed. Meat, fish, and preparations rich in fat hold an important place, while thick soups and preserved foods allow families to be fed when fresh resources become scarce. Plants gathered during favourable periods may supplement the diet, particularly when they provide appreciated flavours or ingredients difficult to obtain during winter. Culinary habits vary between communities, since families living near rivers have greater access to fish, while those of the highlands depend more closely upon hunting and commerce. Certain dishes are associated with family gatherings or celebrations, especially when their preparation requires ingredients reserved for important occasions.

Waste is generally frowned upon. A provision lost in autumn may be sorely missed several months later, particularly when a storm prevents hunters from reaching the grounds they normally frequent. Children therefore learn very early to respect food, maintain containers, and preserve leftovers that can be employed in other preparations. Craftsmen make objects intended to facilitate storage, while those responsible for provisions regularly inspect their condition. The same attention is given to other materials, notably hides and bones, every part of which may serve a particular purpose. The prosperity of a community thus depends as much upon its ability to obtain resources as upon the manner in which it preserves and distributes them.

Hospitality possesses particular significance in such an environment. A traveller caught in a storm may depend entirely upon the welcome offered by a family, particularly when he knows neither the shelters nor the stores available in the region. The Umli may show great generosity towards those who respect their customs and appreciate the value of the resources offered to them. A merchant known for many years sometimes finds a particularly faithful welcome in a settlement, while a stranger may be invited to present himself before the community's leaders before receiving substantial provisions. Such caution arises from the necessities of life: accommodating several travellers for a prolonged period may considerably alter the stores prepared for winter. Generosity is therefore closely linked to responsibility towards the inhabitants, without these precautions implying general hostility towards strangers.

Communal meals also help maintain relationships between families. They provide opportunities to exchange news, discuss expeditions, and recall the obligations uniting different groups. During the long winter months, common halls accommodate gatherings where elders recount the migrations of their ancestors, while the young learn of decisions concerning forthcoming work. Songs, tales, and certain dances accompany celebrations, particularly when stores are sufficient to permit a period of rest. These gatherings allow the Umli to display a sociability that foreign travellers do not always discover during their earliest encounters, especially when they have known this people chiefly through merchants or guards responsible for watching the mountain passages.

Caverns and Underground Settlements

Most Umli maintain enduring ties with caverns, rocky hills, or small underground settlements. These dwellings provide important protection against winds and extreme temperatures, while allowing the resources needed for communal life to be preserved. Their construction requires precise knowledge of stone, particularly when builders must select sufficiently stable caverns, reinforce weak passages, and prevent water from entering during the thaw. Communities willingly employ natural shelters that can be adapted to their needs, while larger settlements include additional galleries, common halls, and specialised spaces. Work is organised according to available resources, for opening a passage or constructing a support may occupy several families for extended periods.

Ventilation holds an essential place in this architecture. Hearths and forges produce smoke that must be carried away, while deep dwellings require shafts allowing fresh air to circulate. Builders choose openings according to the arrangement of caverns and prevailing winds, taking account of snow accumulations that may obstruct them during storms. Installations must also allow water to drain away, particularly when the spring thaw suddenly increases its flow through cracks in the rock. A well-maintained settlement therefore requires regular inspections, especially in areas near hearths, stores, and passages used daily by the inhabitants.

Entrances are chosen with care. An opening beneath a cliff or behind a rocky spur benefits from natural protection, while certain approaches may be partly concealed by the terrain and seasonal accumulations of snow. Builders must nevertheless avoid locations exposed to rockfalls or avalanches, particularly when access routes remain in use during winter. Passages are sometimes narrow enough to be defended by a small number of guards, and certain communities establish secondary entrances allowing hunters to reach their grounds or inhabitants to access outside stores. These arrangements answer the needs of daily life as much as military concerns, particularly when inhabitants must be able to move despite dangers threatening the surrounding lands.

Inside, spaces are divided according to their functions. Food stores occupy areas where conditions favour preservation, workshops possess the installations necessary for their activities, and families have rooms intended for rest and domestic occupations. Common halls accommodate meals, assemblies, and celebrations, particularly when storms prevent travel between settlements. Galleries are maintained to facilitate the movement of materials, while dangerous passages may be reinforced or closed when their use becomes too hazardous. This organisation requires collective knowledge of the place, for inhabitants must know which areas may be freely used and which remain reserved for work, storage, or defence.

Umli dwellings are generally more modest than the great cities of the Khazâd. Their architecture favours safety, ease of maintenance, and the use of available materials, without excluding works of high quality when craftsmen possess the necessary resources. A passage is widened when it becomes too narrow for transporting merchandise, a gallery reinforced when the rock shows signs of weakness, and an additional hall excavated when several families decide to settle permanently in the same dwelling. Decorative objects, sculptures, and inscriptions may commemorate ancestors or important events, but their presence depends upon the prosperity and traditions of each community. A modest family hearth may preserve memories of great personal value without possessing the monumental halls and prestigious works that distinguish the Dwarven kingdoms.

Some settlements also welcome travellers. A hall near the entrance may allow a merchant to deposit his goods, dry his clothing, and find refuge until favourable weather returns. The inhabitants may repair equipment, exchange provisions, or pass on information concerning neighbouring passages. Such places form important points of contact between distant communities, particularly when routes remain impassable for several months. The Umli thus live at the meeting point of two complementary environments: the surface, where much of the resources necessary for their existence can be found, and the depths of caverns, which protect families, accommodate workshops, and allow the provisions upon which their survival depends to be preserved.

The Crafts of Stone and Metal

Umli craft traditions bear witness to remarkable knowledge of the materials available in northern regions. Stoneworking and metalworking occupy an important place in settlements near the mountains, particularly when communities possess deposits that can be exploited without undertaking long expeditions. Miners learn to identify ores, open galleries, and reinforce passages required for extraction, while those responsible for the work must assess risks and determine the resources that should be devoted to each undertaking. Even a modest mine may represent considerable wealth for a settlement, especially when it provides the metals essential for manufacturing tools and weapons. Its exploitation nevertheless demands precautions, for a collapse, water infiltration, or the deterioration of a support may jeopardise the safety of the workers.

Smiths then transform available materials into objects suited to the needs of their community. They make knives, hunting points, axes, weapons, and the parts required to maintain equipment, but also devote a substantial part of their work to repairs. In a region far removed from major trading centres, a broken blade, unusable tool, or damaged fastening may jeopardise an entire expedition. Craftsmen therefore attach great importance to strength, precision, and the possibility of replacing individual parts without having to manufacture the whole object anew. Masters pass on their techniques to apprentices, particularly when a method extends the useful life of equipment whose materials are difficult to obtain.

Forging, however, requires particular care among the Umli, whose constitution tolerates great heat poorly. Workshops must be organised to limit risks, especially when several furnaces operate simultaneously or prolonged work makes the air difficult to breathe. Craftsmen learn to control temperatures, protect their clothing, and interrupt certain operations when their physical condition requires it. Their natural resistance to cold offers little help against the radiant heat of the furnaces, and the quality of their work depends chiefly upon the technical knowledge acquired during their training. This necessity makes the mastery of fire a demanding discipline, in which safety precautions hold as much importance as manual skill.

Stonemasons also participate in maintaining dwellings. They construct steps, doorframes, shafts, and supporting structures, while watching for signs of weakness in the rock. Their work generally favours the strength and durability of installations, particularly when a passage must remain usable throughout harsh winters. Certain craftsmen nevertheless possess a pronounced taste for ornamentation and devote part of their time to carving objects intended for family ceremonies or the preservation of ancestral memory. Their works may thus unite practical requirements with symbolic significance, especially when an engraved stone commemorates the founding of a settlement or a door bears the marks of the families who took part in its construction.

Professional reputation plays an important role in these communities. A skilled craftsman may be known far beyond his settlement and receive commissions from neighbouring groups, particularly when his work withstands difficult conditions better than that of his competitors. Relations with the Khazâd sometimes encourage exchanges of knowledge, while merchandise arriving from human regions provides materials unavailable to the Umli locally. Some masters agree to teach their methods to foreign apprentices, while others prefer to preserve techniques particular to their families. These differences bear witness to craft traditions developed over a long history, whose achievements remain deeply connected with the necessities of the Far North.

Working Hides, Bone, and Ordinary Materials

Working hides occupies an essential place in Umli life, particularly when clothing must protect inhabitants during long periods of exposure to cold. Craftsmen select furs and leathers according to their properties, prepare the materials, and make cloaks, footwear, blankets, and accessories suited to the activities of their community. Clothing intended for hunting must allow freedom of movement while retaining the necessary warmth, whereas garments worn in mines must withstand abrasion and protect certain parts of the body. Seams are reinforced where they receive the greatest strain, and worn sections may be replaced when the rest of the article remains serviceable. A well-made piece of equipment may represent several weeks of work, explaining the care devoted to its maintenance.

Children learn at an early age to recognise defects in clothing and understand the importance of completing repairs before an expedition departs. An open seam may admit wind or snow, while badly fitting footwear may cause injuries during a long march. Families therefore preserve tools suited to leatherworking, particularly needles, awls, and cords allowing simple repairs to be carried out. Specialist craftsmen make the more complex articles, especially those intended to protect travellers exposed to extreme conditions. Commercial exchanges may provide fabrics or foreign materials, but their use sometimes requires adaptation to the particular needs of the Umli.

Bone, wood, and sinew constitute other valuable resources. They are used to make needles, handles, parts of traps, utensils, and numerous small objects required in everyday life. Craftsmen know the properties of each material and choose those most suitable for the intended purpose, particularly when an object must retain its strength despite moisture or changes in temperature. Repairs occupy a substantial part of their work, for a tool whose metal component remains intact can be returned to use after its handle or fastenings have been replaced. This habit of preserving and maintaining objects reflects an economy in which resources are valuable and opportunities to replace them sometimes limited.

Certain craftsmen also produce ornaments and objects intended for family ceremonies. A piece of engraved bone may commemorate an important expedition, a metal buckle bear the mark of a family, and a knife presented to an apprentice signify the completion of his training. Garments readily retain the natural colours of their materials, particularly the beige of hides, the grey of furs, and the brown shades of leather, but families may also employ ornaments or patterns associated with their traditions. Such objects do not necessarily possess great commercial value, especially when made from ordinary materials, but their personal significance may be considerable. A character may preserve throughout his life a tool received from his master or an object made by a departed relative, its possession recalling the bonds connecting him with his lat.

Roads and Commercial Relations

The Umli maintain commercial relationships with the populations of the Far North, particularly when their resources allow them to produce goods sought by their neighbours. Hides, tools, weapons, metal objects, and certain materials may be exchanged for salt, provisions, fabrics, or products difficult to obtain in the frozen regions. Such relations remain strongly influenced by the seasons, since storms and the condition of passages considerably limit travel during certain periods. Merchants must therefore prepare their routes, know the stopping places, and determine the quantities they can transport without jeopardising their safety. A trading expedition demands precise organisation, particularly when it includes several families or must cross territories far from familiar settlements.

Trading partners may maintain relationships extending across several generations. An Umli merchant may know the parents and descendants of a Lossadan family, preserve memories of contracts concluded decades earlier, and regularly return to the same places of exchange. Such continuity encourages trust when commitments are honoured, but may also make disagreements difficult to overcome. Goods whose quality was disputed, a postponed payment, or an ancient debt may remain present in relations between two families, particularly when the individuals concerned personally remember the circumstances. Experienced traders therefore learn to establish the terms of agreements precisely and recognise the customs of the communities they frequent.

Trade routes also allow information to circulate. A traveller brings news of storms, herd movements, the presence of hostile bands, or changes affecting neighbouring settlements. Such information may prove as valuable as the merchandise carried, especially when it allows a community to alter its expeditions or strengthen the watch over a passage. Umli who regularly travel the roads sometimes know several languages and possess extensive experience of foreign traditions, while those who remain in the most isolated settlements have much more limited knowledge. A character may thus have grown up among traders and become familiar with Lossoth customs without possessing the experience of a hunter capable of crossing the wilderness alone.

Contact with more southerly kingdoms remains relatively rare, particularly when distances make expeditions costly and dangerous. Certain Umli nevertheless undertake long journeys in search of materials, new partners, or knowledge absent from their communities. Their travels may bring them among the Khazâd, to human settlements of the North, or towards the lands of Eriador, where their appearance and habits sometimes arouse curiosity. Such experiences encourage the learning of new trades and languages, but also demand adaptation to the climates and institutions of the regions crossed. A trader accustomed to agreements between tali and umlati may discover very different commercial rules in a human city, while a craftsman must learn to assess the materials and techniques employed by peoples whose works he previously knew only through stories.

The Umitic Language and the Transmission of Knowledge

The Umli possess their own language, Umitic, for which MERP developments also describe a written form. It serves family relationships, exchanges between communities, and the transmission of knowledge concerning trades, territories, and genealogies. Place-names occupy an important place in their memory, particularly when they commemorate an ancient expedition, the founding of a settlement, or the circumstances of an encounter. A valley may bear the name of a hunter who discovered a passage there, while a cavern preserves that of the family who prepared it for habitation several generations earlier. Such names connect practical knowledge with collective memory and facilitate the transmission of routes between elders and young guides.

Paths are often described through natural landmarks whose significance escapes foreign travellers. An isolated rock, a characteristic slope, a watercourse, or a stand of trees that withstands storms may enable a route to be recognised even when snow has erased the tracks. Such directions require thorough knowledge of the land, particularly when the appearance of the terrain changes with the seasons. An elder may describe a passage by recalling events that occurred at several points along it, while a young guide gradually learns to associate these accounts with the places he crosses. Written documents supplement this knowledge but cannot replace direct experience, especially when weather conditions rapidly alter the safety of a route.

The Umli generally appreciate precise accounts, particularly when they concern events whose knowledge may prove useful to future generations. Elders recount family migrations, alliances concluded with neighbouring communities, hunting expeditions, and incidents that occurred in mines. They preserve memories of particularly severe winters, passages abandoned after collapses, and techniques that allowed damaged works to be repaired. Such stories contribute to the education of the young and help sustain collective memory, particularly when families must make decisions concerning territories whose customs reach back several generations. The tale of Sinuphel, Ucin, and Ulaphel holds a special place among these traditions, connecting contemporary communities with the legendary origins of their people.

Song and dance also accompany family gatherings, celebrations, and periods of rest. Some compositions recall ancient migrations, the exploits of hunters, or the founding of settlements, while others celebrate unions, reunions, and works accomplished together. Variations between communities reflect the relationships they maintain and the events that have marked their history, particularly when families long separated meet again during an assembly. Engraved objects, inherited tools, and inscriptions preserved within dwellings provide other means of sustaining these memories. A character may therefore know many tales of his people without having learned to read, while an Umli scholar may devote his life to gathering the written and oral traditions of several settlements.

Commercial exchanges encourage the learning of foreign languages. Labba may be useful in relations with the Lossoth, while Westron facilitates conversations with travellers from the West. Some Umli know words or expressions in Khuzdul, particularly when they have studied under a Dwarven craftsman or taken part in negotiations with the Khazâd. Other northern languages, notably Logathig and Bethteur, may be learned according to the regions visited and the communities encountered. Mastery of these tongues remains dependent upon upbringing and personal experience, for membership of the Umli Race grants no automatic knowledge of all the languages of the Far North.

Mahlic and the Memory of the Ancestors

The spiritual traditions of the Umli reflect their cultural closeness to the Khazâd and the human peoples of the North. According to the developments of MERP, they acknowledge Eru Ilúvatar and the Valar, while according particular importance to Aulë, whom they call Mahlic. The Vala associated with stone, metals, and the arts of making possesses profound significance for a people whose existence depends upon mastery of materials and the maintenance of underground settlements. Respect for Mahlic finds expression especially in the quality of work, the transmission of trades, and certain practices accompanying important events in communal life. A craftsman may regard the creation of a sturdy tool as a way of honouring the teachings he has received, particularly when his work directly contributes to his family's safety.

The opening of a gallery, the commissioning of a forge, or the completion of a particularly difficult work may give rise to gatherings and solemn words. Families then recall the efforts made, the dangers overcome, and the people who took part in the undertaking. Certain settlements preserve tools used during major enterprises, particularly when they were handed down by masters whose memory remains important. A hammer may recall the craftsman who used it for several decades, while an engraved stone preserves the name of a worker associated with the founding of a dwelling. Such objects are not necessarily magical in nature, but constitute material testimony to knowledge and commitments passed down through generations.

The memory of ancestors occupies an essential place in these traditions. Families preserve the names of those who discovered new passages, founded the earliest settlements, or protected their loved ones during times of danger. Their stories may be passed down within the tali, particularly when several branches of the same kindred gather to recall events from their shared history. Some communities attach great importance to formal ceremonies, while others chiefly express respect through domestic customs, songs, and the maintenance of ancient places. These differences allow characters to develop varied personal relationships with their people's heritage, particularly when they have grown up in settlements possessing distinct traditions.

Fire occupies a singular place in this relationship with Mahlic. It warms dwellings, cooks food, and transforms metals, but also represents a considerable danger for a people whose constitution remains vulnerable to high temperatures. Craftsmen therefore learn to maintain hearths with precision, protect fuel stores, and prevent accidents that might threaten the inhabitants. Such mastery requires practical knowledge, whose transmission occupies an important place in workshops. Respect for fire may thus be understood as respect for an indispensable tool whose use carries responsibility for everyone, particularly when several families depend upon the same hearth or installation.

These traditions belong to the developments of MERP and enrich the spiritual identity of the Umli without establishing any new lineage in Tolkien's writings. They must not be confused with automatic possession of magical powers, particularly when characters practise a craft associated with Mahlic. A smith may know the techniques of his art without mastering a single spell, while a character drawn to magical disciplines must have received the corresponding instruction. In MERP-UI, access to Essence, Mentalism, Channeling, and other realms of magic remains subject to the compatibilities of Culture and Profession, together with RMU rules.

Dragons, Wargs, and the Dangers of the Frozen Lands

The Umli preserve a particularly deep hostility towards Dragons and Wargs, whose threats occupy an important place in their traditions. The memory of Lamthanc, the Cold-drake who is said to have killed Sinuphel, belongs to their founding tale and recalls the dangers faced by the earliest generations. Dragons represent enemies capable of destroying stores, devastating settlements, and forcing inhabitants to abandon lands occupied for generations. Cold-drakes are especially feared in the northern regions, where their presence may render mountain passages dangerous and jeopardise the exploitation of resources needed by communities. Accounts of their appearance lead leaders to watch ancient caverns, mountain passes, and territories whose inhabitants report unusual disappearances.

Wargs constitute a more frequent threat to travellers and small settlements. Their packs may pursue hunters, attack isolated individuals, and make certain routes dangerous during seasons when resources become scarce. The Umli therefore attach great importance to tracking and watching the surrounding lands, particularly when they discover traces in the snow indicating the recent passage of several animals. Guides must learn to recognise signs announcing the proximity of a pack and choose routes that limit the risks faced by their companions. When a threat is reported, inhabitants may strengthen the watch, postpone an expedition, or prepare the approaches to their dwelling in order to protect the most vulnerable families.

Orcs also represent a danger, particularly when their bands travel through the mountains or seek to seize resources held by isolated settlements. Communities must then rely upon their knowledge of the terrain and the preparation of defensive positions suited to their stature and numbers. Narrow passages, difficult slopes, and natural obstacles may reduce the advantage of larger opponents, while guarded approaches allow a threat to be recognised before it reaches the dwellings. Galleries and cavern entrances may also be arranged to slow attackers, particularly when inhabitants have sufficient time to prepare their defences.

Umli warriors employ weapons suited to their constitution and the activities of their people. Axes, hammers, maces, short swords, spears, and knives are among their possible equipment, while bows, slings, and thrown weapons allow them to fight at a distance. Harpoons may also be employed according to circumstances, particularly among populations whose occupations make them familiar. Protection depends upon climate and the demands of the mission. Thick clothing and reinforced leather suit long expeditions, while warriors responsible for defending the entrances to a dwelling may wear heavier equipment. Such choices must nevertheless take account of fatigue and temperature, particularly when prolonged use of armour restricts movement or causes excessive heat.

Defending a settlement remains above all a collective undertaking. Stores must be protected, secondary entrances watched, and the most vulnerable inhabitants brought to safe areas when danger approaches. Those responsible for construction may seal certain passages, guides identify routes suitable for evacuation, and craftsmen prepare equipment needed by the defenders. Military experience varies between individuals. A hunter who has spent several decades travelling through threatened regions may possess extensive knowledge of ambushes and tracking, while a smith established in a peaceful community may have received only the training needed for local defence. The robustness of the Umli constitutes an advantage, but the skills that allow them to confront their enemies always arise from training and situations they have personally experienced.

Among the Other Peoples of Middle-earth

The relationships of the Umli with other peoples are profoundly influenced by their distance from the great kingdoms and by the necessities of their existence. The Lossoth number among their most familiar neighbours, particularly in regions where the two peoples frequent nearby territories and depend upon comparable resources. They share extensive knowledge of the hardships of the Far North, travel across snow, and the dangers associated with changing weather. Exchanges concern hides, tools, food, metals, and products that each community can obtain more readily than its neighbours. Information concerning storms, the movements of animals, or the condition of passages also possesses great value, particularly when several groups must prepare their expeditions according to the same climatic conditions.

These relationships may be lasting and friendly, but are sometimes marked by rivalries concerning hunting grounds, fishing places, or resources required by settlements. An Umli family may have maintained regular exchanges with a Lossadan group for several generations, while another preserves the memory of an ancient dispute whose circumstances are no longer perfectly known. Marriage and kinship also occupy a particular place in the founding tale of the Umli, especially through Ulaphel's union with a Lossoth hunter. Characters raised in neighbouring communities may therefore possess extensive knowledge of one another's customs, while those who grew up in isolated regions know them chiefly through stories passed on by merchants.

Relations with the Khazâd possess a different dimension. The Umli regard them as possible distant relatives, associated with the legendary history of their origins, and readily acknowledge their mastery of stone and metals. Craftsmen of the two peoples may compare techniques, exchange materials, and take part in common enterprises, particularly when their settlements maintain regular commercial relationships. Some Umli learn expressions in Khuzdul or receive instruction from a Dwarven master, while the Khazâd may appreciate the particular knowledge of their neighbours concerning materials and conditions found in the frozen regions. Such relations do not, however, erase the differences between their peoples. The Umli possess their own lineages, customs, and institutions, and may resent the condescension of a Dwarf who regards them as imperfect descendants of his people.

The Men of the North generally know the Umli through travellers' tales and commercial relations maintained with certain communities. Their small stature, appearance, and resistance to cold may arouse curiosity, while their craftsmanship earns the respect of those who regularly use their tools. The Dúnedain and inhabitants of more southerly kingdoms seldom encounter them in their homeland, particularly when distances and climatic conditions make expeditions difficult. Those who nevertheless undertake journeys through the Far North may appreciate the experience of Umli guides, their knowledge of shelters, and their ability to provide suitable equipment. A character may thus become a particularly valuable companion to foreign travellers, while discovering among the southern kingdoms institutions and customs of which he previously knew almost nothing.

The Elves remain relatively distant from most Umli communities. Encounters are exceptional and may arouse mutual curiosity, particularly when the individuals know little of one another's traditions or languages. An Umit may know the Quendi chiefly through travellers' accounts, while an Elf who has long lived in the western lands may never have encountered a Half-dwarf. Exchanges of knowledge may nevertheless prove fruitful, particularly when a character wishes to understand plants, languages, or the ancient migrations of northern peoples. Differences in longevity, traditions, and their relationship with the world may give rise to unusual friendships, especially when individuals gradually learn to recognise the qualities of their companions.

Conflicts affecting neighbouring regions may also reach the Umli, even when their communities remain far from great political centres. A war may interrupt a commercial route, cause populations to move, or bring armed bands into territories that had previously been relatively safe. The inhabitants must then decide whether to strengthen their defences, welcome refugees, or seek new alliances. Their opposition to Dragons, Wargs, and the other servants of the Shadow may bring them closer to peoples pursuing the same objectives, particularly when protecting roads and settlements requires enduring cooperation. Such circumstances offer characters many opportunities to discover the wider world without necessarily abandoning the responsibilities binding them to their community.

The Umli Through the Ages

The history of the Umli is difficult to place precisely within the chronology of the earliest Ages of Middle-earth. Their founding tale mentions the lands of Hildórien and events dating back to the origins of the first Men, but MERP traditions do not allow the formation of their earliest communities to be dated with certainty. During the First Age, the existence of an already established Umli people cannot therefore be regarded as certain, and the creation of a character belonging to this period requires particular justification. The Gamemaster may choose to explore their legendary origins or imagine the earliest migrations of families destined to give rise to their people, but such developments belong to a particular interpretation of the game setting rather than directly documented history.

During the Second Age, the northern regions undergo changes connected with migrations and events affecting the peoples of Middle-earth. Umli traditions may be imagined as ancient, particularly when family tales mention settlements and lineages reaching back to a distant time. The available material remains insufficient, however, to establish precisely their territories, institutions, or relationships with other peoples during this period. A character from this Age must therefore be conceived with caution, taking account of the limits of information provided by MERP and the choices particular to the campaign. He may belong to a community established in the cold northern regions, but its specific traditions will need to be defined in agreement with the Gamemaster.

During the Third Age, the Umli can be incorporated more directly into the developments devoted to the northern lands. Their communities occupy the regions of Ûrd, Uab, and certain neighbouring territories of Forodwaith, while relations with the Lossoth, Khazâd, and other northern populations provide the setting for their activities. Migrations, climatic difficulties, and local conflicts may cause certain settlements to disappear or relocate, while others develop relatively prosperous mining or trading activities. A character may therefore grow up within an ancient community, participate in founding a new home, or belong to a family whose members preserve the memory of several migrations. Threats from Dragons, Wargs, and Orcs may likewise lead inhabitants to undertake military expeditions or seek the assistance of their neighbours.

During the Fourth Age, the political transformations following Sauron's disappearance may alter relations between the peoples of the North. The restoration of the kingdoms of the Dúnedain and the gradual improvement of certain routes open new prospects for communities wishing to develop their exchanges, particularly when formerly threatened regions become safer. The Umli may participate in these enterprises by providing guides, craftsmen, or goods suited to northern conditions, while others prefer to preserve the customs of their traditional settlements. Ancient rivalries do not necessarily disappear with the end of the great wars, especially when they concern territories or family commitments. This period nevertheless offers important possibilities for characters wishing to discover the wider world, renew interrupted relationships, or help rebuild a community weakened by earlier events.

Perseverance and Responsibilities Towards the Home

In MERP traditions, the Umli are often described as reserved, stubborn, fierce, and deeply attached to their possessions and commitments. These dispositions should be understood through the concrete conditions of their existence. A well-made tool may represent several weeks of work, a supply of food require months of preparation, and an underground dwelling result from efforts continued over several generations. Possession of such goods brings responsibility towards those who depend upon them, particularly when their loss might jeopardise the safety of an entire family. An Umit may therefore take great care of an ancient knife, a pair of skis, or a chest of tools, not necessarily because he seeks wealth, but because he understands the labour involved in making them and the difficulties their loss would cause.

Caution towards strangers likewise arises from this experience. A community that has calculated its stores to survive a long winter cannot accommodate large numbers of visitors indefinitely without compromising its own needs. Its leaders must therefore assess the resources available, the circumstances in which travellers have arrived, and the possibility of obtaining fresh provisions before offering a prolonged stay. Such reserve may be interpreted as mistrust by foreigners accustomed to more prosperous regions, particularly when they do not understand the constraints imposed by the climate. The Umli may nevertheless show great generosity towards those who respect their customs and acknowledge the value of the assistance received, especially when the memory of an earlier act of help already connects their families.

Their perseverance is apparent in everyday activities. A craftsman may patiently rework an object until he achieves the desired result, a hunter follow tracks for several days, and a community leader devote years to preparing the establishment of several families in a new territory. Such constancy favours the success of difficult undertakings, but may become obstinacy when circumstances demand swift change. An elder may refuse to abandon a threatened dwelling because several generations have worked there, while a master preserves a method that has become less effective out of loyalty to the teachings he received. Younger members may wish to adopt new techniques or develop relations with foreign peoples, particularly when they believe such changes will improve the living conditions of their community.

Individuals nevertheless respond very differently to inherited traditions. Some gladly seek the company of travellers and learn their languages, while others prefer to remain within their community and devote their lives to a familiar trade. A young Umit may wish to discover the great human cities, an experienced huntress undertake the exploration of unknown territories, and an elder choose to travel no longer after several difficult migrations. Some enjoy festivals, songs, and family gatherings, particularly when reunited with relatives from whom they have long been separated. Others remain more reserved, attached to solitary activities or work requiring great concentration. The heritage of the Umli provides habits and points of reference, but personal experience determines how each individual chooses to employ them.

Playing an Umit

Playing an Umit in Middle-earth means portraying a character belonging to a rare people whose identity is rooted in a family, a territory, and traditions developed through long generations spent in the frozen lands of the North. His appearance and constitution recall the Khazâd, while his customs and history also connect him with the human populations with whom his ancestors are said to have maintained relationships. This dual affinity gives him a particular place among the peoples of Middle-earth, but determines neither his vocation nor his temperament. An Umit may have grown up in a community of hunters, among the craftsmen of an underground settlement, or within a family of merchants whose journeys sustain exchanges between several valleys. His upbringing determines the knowledge he actually possesses, especially when he leaves for the first time the territories where his relatives have lived for generations.

A young Umit may have grown up in a cavern adapted for habitation near a river. He knows the paths followed by hunters, the places where fish gather during certain seasons, and the precautions necessary when crossing frozen ground. His parents have taught him to prepare clothing, watch over stores, and recognise signs announcing a storm, but his knowledge of more distant territories remains limited. His departure may be motivated by the search for a missing relative, a commercial mission, or the desire to discover regions beyond familiar lands. He may also have received a specific task from his umlat, particularly when a community wishes to rediscover an ancient passage or verify information brought by travellers. Skills acquired during childhood will prove valuable, but he must learn to confront situations very different from those he knew in his valley.

Another character may belong to a mining community, where underground work occupies an important place in daily life. He has learned to identify ores, maintain tools, and understand the dangers of galleries, particularly as his master gradually entrusted him with responsibilities concerning their safety. He may have participated in opening a new passage, repairing an ancient installation, or searching for materials that have become difficult to obtain. His adventure may begin when a craftsman sends him to negotiate an agreement with Khazâd smiths, seek a particular ore, or recover a manufacturing process preserved in the traditions of a distant family. The journey will allow him to compare the techniques of his people with those of other communities, while forcing him to adapt to the customs of negotiation and climatic conditions of the regions he crosses.

A female Umit from a group of hunters may possess remarkable knowledge of animals, tracks, and changing weather. She knows how to prepare a camp, organise provisions, and choose a safe passage when conditions become difficult. Her experience may make her a guide sought after by travellers less familiar with the North, particularly when they must cross territories where routes exist only during certain seasons. She may have learned her trade from an experienced relative, accompanied several expeditions, and participated in protecting her community's stores. Her departure may arise from a mission entrusted to her by her lat, the search for a missing group, or the desire to discover lands whose resources might allow new families to settle. She possesses valuable knowledge, but may be bewildered by the customs of a great city, particularly when decisions depend upon officials and contracts whose rules she does not understand.

An older character may have experienced several migrations. He preserves the memory of an abandoned dwelling, a lost territory, or an alliance concluded with a neighbouring community whose descendants now live far from their former region. He may have devoted part of his life to maintaining a workshop, participated in defending a settlement, and continued exchanges with human families whose generations have succeeded one another. His adventure may be motivated by the desire to recover ancient property, renew interrupted relations, or pass on to his descendants knowledge threatened with disappearance. His extensive experience allows him to recognise certain changes in the world, but does not mean he possesses mastery of every skill. A craftsman may know the techniques of his forge perfectly while remaining ignorant of the hunting practices of neighbouring communities, whereas an experienced guide may possess only limited knowledge of foreign languages.

Family affiliations provide an important source of roleplaying possibilities. The character belongs to a lat, whose principal lineages he knows, and may also have obligations towards the umlat bringing together the inhabitants of his region. These two affiliations offer valuable support, particularly when he must find shelter, obtain an apprenticeship, or seek help from distant relatives. They may nevertheless give rise to expectations difficult to satisfy when he wishes to lead a different life from the one his relatives have prepared for him. A character may agree to depart in fulfilment of a family obligation, then discover during his journey possibilities he had never considered. Another may seek independence while retaining profound affection for those whose lives he has long shared.

Relationships with the Khazâd deserve particular consideration. An Umit may regard the Dwarves as distant relatives, admire their achievements, or wish to understand the techniques employed in their great workshops. He may also feel deep irritation when a Khazâd treats his people with condescension, particularly when such an attitude disregards the particular knowledge the Umli have developed to survive in the Far North. A character may have studied under a Dwarven master and remain deeply loyal to him, while another possesses less favourable memories arising from a commercial dispute or rivalry concerning a mine. These experiences lend personal depth to his relationships with the Khazâd, without imposing identical admiration or hostility upon all Umli.

The Lossoth and other peoples of the North may represent trading partners, familiar neighbours, or communities with which his family maintains ancient disputes. A character who grew up near their territories knows their languages and customs far better than an Umit raised in an isolated region, particularly when he has participated in exchanges of goods or seasonal journeys. He may preserve old friendships, know several families, and possess commitments whose importance will become apparent during his adventures. Relationships with more southerly Men may be different, especially when travellers regard his people as a curiosity or know nothing of their traditions. Such encounters offer opportunities to develop his knowledge and reconsider certain convictions inherited from his upbringing.

Departure for warmer countries constitutes a particularly important experience. An Umit accustomed to frozen regions must learn to choose different clothing, alter his travelling hours, and organise his exertions to avoid the consequences of high temperatures. Heat that seems tolerable to his companions may become a genuine ordeal for him, particularly when he must wear armour or march for long hours beneath the Sun. He may seek mountainous regions, shaded routes, and places where he can rest under suitable conditions. Conversely, his natural qualities become especially valuable when an expedition crosses frozen lands, particularly when the other members of the group possess no experience of travelling across snow.

His practical skills may find many applications during adventures. An Umit may know how to maintain a blade, repair clothing, recognise certain materials, organise provisions, or identify signs of changing weather. A hunter possesses knowledge of animals and tracks, while a craftsman understands the properties of tools and the risks associated with their use. A guide may rediscover a safe passage or choose shelter suited to the conditions, particularly when the group crosses a territory whose dangers escape the other travellers. Such abilities are not necessarily spectacular, but may prove decisive when resources are limited and survival depends upon practical decisions made at the right moment.

The character's Profession provides another important source of roleplaying possibilities. A Fighter may have received training intended for the defence of settlements, particularly when a community must protect its stores and passages against Wargs or Orcs. A Ranger may possess thorough knowledge of northern territories, animal migrations, and the techniques required for travelling through the wilderness. A Rogue may have developed his skills during commercial journeys, reconnaissance, or missions demanding great caution, while a Thief may have learned to negotiate narrow passages, observe the habits of guards, or manipulate mechanisms encountered in foreign settlements. A Bard may devote his life to the tales of Sinuphel, Ucin, and Ulaphel, together with the preservation of genealogies, languages, and the traditions of his people.

Other Professions may be considered according to the compatibilities established by MERP-UI, particularly when a character has received instruction under a master or within a community possessing the necessary knowledge. A craftsman may wish to deepen the techniques associated with Mahlic, while a scholar seeks to understand the origins of his people or compare traditions preserved in several settlements. Magical arts may likewise be studied when Culture, Profession, and the instruction received permit them, in accordance with RMU rules. The spiritual traditions of the Umli and their legendary mixed ancestry nevertheless grant no automatic access to disciplines reserved for other peoples, particularly when certain Professions remain exclusively associated with the Khazâd or communities possessing their own institutions.

The memory of Sinuphel, Ucin, and Ulaphel may nourish important personal motivations. Some characters regard these figures as the true ancestors of their people and wish to rediscover traces of their journeys, particularly the places where they are said to have established their earliest dwellings. Others are more interested in the values passed down through the tales and seek to understand why certain families preserve different versions. An Umit may undertake a search for Lamthanc's former lair, seek documents concerning the earliest migrations, or gather the testimony of distant communities. Such enterprises may lead him through regions whose dangers were described in the traditions of his childhood, but whose reality may have changed profoundly since the events recounted.

A character may also be led to leave his home for entirely personal reasons. He may have grown up in a prosperous settlement, practised a respected trade, and never wished to travel until a particular event transformed his circumstances. The disappearance of a loved one, the interruption of commerce, the destruction of a store, or the need to find a master may compel him to undertake a long journey. He may wish to protect his companions, recover a precious object, or make amends for a mistake whose consequences threaten several families. His attachment to home then lends particular depth to his decision, for departure separates him from the people, habits, and responsibilities that have shaped his entire existence.

The choice of Age must finally remain consistent with the available material. During the First and Second Ages, the origins and organisation of the Umli are insufficiently known to allow an ordinary representation of their people without particular development by the Gamemaster. During the Third Age, a character may belong to the communities described in the northern lands, participate in relations with the Lossoth and Khazâd, or continue family traditions associated with ancient settlements. During the Fourth Age, he may benefit from new commercial opportunities, participate in founding a community, or undertake the exploration of territories made more accessible by the political transformations of Middle-earth. Each period influences relations with other peoples, the events preserved in family memory, and the prospects that may lead the character to embark upon an adventure.

The Umli — Half-dwarves Race is offered in MERP-UI principally during the Third and Fourth Ages of Middle-earth. It remains restricted because of its rarity, particular origins, and pronounced physical adaptations. It represents the fundamental characteristics shared by the Umli: their small stature, robustness, longevity, exceptional resistance to cold, vulnerability to heat, and reduced need for sleep. These dispositions belong exclusively to Race and must retain the values and mechanics already defined within the module.

The choice of the Umli Culture then determines the knowledge acquired in their environment, including survival in the tundra, hunting, fishing, tracking, caving, metalworking, working leather and bone, languages, and traditions associated with Mahlic. Professional possibilities remain subject to MERP-UI compatibility rules, without the people's legendary origins automatically allowing access to Professions particular to the Khazâd or other communities. Before approving character creation, the player and Gamemaster should establish the character's homeland, family, possible membership of a lat and an umlat, original occupation, his community's relations with the Lossoth and Khazâd, and the circumstances that led him to leave the northern lands.

These choices should give him a tangible history, personal attachments, and responsibilities whose consequences may emerge throughout his adventures. An Umit may wish to preserve a dwelling, find a missing family, deepen his knowledge, honour a commitment, or build a life different from the one his relatives had prepared for him. His heritage offers remarkable knowledge and natural dispositions, but he remains free to decide how he will employ his qualities and what relationships he wishes to maintain with other peoples.

An Umit inherits from his ancestors knowledge of the frozen lands, the patience of work carefully accomplished, and the memory of generations who survived before him. His constitution enables him to face formidable conditions, while his upbringing passes on the knowledge necessary to protect his loved ones and maintain the dwellings of his family. The roads he travels, the alliances he chooses, and the works he leaves behind will determine what he contributes to the history of his people, whether he one day returns to his kin or continues his life beyond the lands of the Far North.

talents.description: Les Umli bénéficient d’une forte résistance au froid et à la glace, mais supportent mal les chaleurs extrêmes.

talents.name: Efficient Sleeper
talents.description: Trois heures de sommeil suffisent normalement à leur récupération.

talents.name: Nightvision
talents.description: Ils voient efficacement dans la pénombre et les cavernes faiblement éclairées.

talents.name: Compact Build
talents.description: Leur ossature dense et leur centre de gravité bas leur donnent une grande stabilité.

system.description:
Umli — Les Demi-Nains

Avant le lever du jour, dans une caverne des hautes terres du Nord, une femme examine les provisions disposées sur des claies de bois. Elle vérifie les pièces de viande suspendues près du conduit de fumée, écarte une peau dont les coutures ont commencé à se défaire et demande à son fils de rapporter les outils laissés dans l'atelier. Dehors, le vent soulève la neige contre les rochers et efface progressivement les traces du chemin. Une expédition de chasse doit partir dès que la lumière permettra de distinguer les pentes, mais les dernières bourrasques pourraient contraindre les chasseurs à modifier leur itinéraire. La femme consulte les marques tracées sur une tablette de bois, où sont consignées les quantités de viande, de graisse et de poisson conservées depuis l'automne. Les réserves permettront encore de nourrir les familles pendant plusieurs semaines, à condition que les sorties prochaines rapportent suffisamment de gibier. Son père, qui a connu des hivers plus rigoureux encore, lui conseille de conserver une partie des provisions les mieux protégées jusqu'au retour du dégel. Elle acquiesce, puis rejoint les chasseurs rassemblés près de l'entrée afin de leur indiquer les besoins des familles. Lorsque l'expédition disparaît derrière la première crête, elle retourne auprès du foyer où les plus jeunes préparent les vêtements qui devront être réparés avant leur prochain départ.

Plus loin vers l'est, dans un établissement creusé à flanc de montagne, un forgeron termine la réparation d'une lame destinée à un marchand lossadan. La chaleur du foyer lui rougit le visage, mais il travaille avec précision, surveillant la couleur du métal avant de le plonger dans l'eau. Son client attend près de l'entrée de l'atelier, enveloppé dans un épais manteau de fourrure. Les deux hommes se connaissent depuis plusieurs années. Ils ont traversé ensemble des passages difficiles, échangé des marchandises et partagé leurs réserves lorsque les tempêtes rendaient tout voyage impossible. Le forgeron lui remet enfin la lame, accompagnée d'un fourreau neuf dont les coutures ont été renforcées pour résister à l'humidité. Le paiement avait été convenu à l'automne précédent : plusieurs peaux, du sel et une provision de poisson séché. Avant de quitter l'atelier, le marchand déploie une carte grossièrement dessinée sur un morceau de cuir et demande si le passage méridional demeure praticable. Le forgeron lui conseille de suivre une autre vallée, où des chasseurs ont récemment signalé l'effondrement d'une corniche. Il lui confie également un petit paquet destiné à une famille établie au-delà du col, dont il attend des nouvelles depuis la fin de l'été.

À plusieurs journées de marche, une jeune Umit conduit deux voyageurs humains vers un établissement dont ils ignorent l'emplacement. Leurs vêtements sont adaptés aux régions tempérées, et leurs bottes commencent à laisser pénétrer l'eau de la neige fondue. Elle leur a imposé une halte avant le passage d'un plateau exposé au vent, puis a distribué les cordages qu'elle avait préparés pour la traversée. Les étrangers auraient préféré poursuivre leur marche, mais les nuages qui s'accumulent derrière les montagnes annoncent une dégradation rapide du temps. Elle connaît les passages protégés, les creux où la neige devient dangereusement profonde et les abris utilisés par les chasseurs pendant leurs expéditions. Son grand-père lui enseigna ces itinéraires lorsqu'elle était enfant, et les marques laissées par les voyageurs des générations précédentes lui permettent encore de reconnaître les chemins lorsque les traces récentes ont disparu. Avant la tombée du jour, elle retrouve l'entrée d'une ancienne caverne, dégage la neige accumulée contre la pierre et conduit ses compagnons à l'intérieur. Tandis qu'ils retirent leurs vêtements trempés, elle prépare le foyer et examine les provisions disponibles. Le lendemain, si la tempête s'est apaisée, ils pourront rejoindre les habitants de la vallée suivante.

Tous appartiennent aux Umli, un peuple rare que les voyageurs désignent parfois sous le nom de Demi-Nains. Leur petite stature, leur robustesse et certains de leurs traits rappellent les Khazâd, tandis que leurs traditions les rattachent également aux peuples humains du Grand Nord. Ils habitent des territoires où les hivers peuvent interrompre les communications pendant plusieurs semaines, où la connaissance d'un passage sûr possède une valeur considérable et où la conservation des provisions détermine souvent la sécurité des familles. Leurs communautés possèdent leurs propres lignées, leur langue, leurs établissements et des institutions adaptées à la dispersion des ressources. Certains Umli se consacrent à la chasse, à la pêche et aux déplacements saisonniers, tandis que d'autres travaillent la pierre, exploitent les minerais ou entretiennent des relations commerciales avec les peuples voisins. Leur histoire, développée dans les traditions de MERP, est celle d'une population qui a appris à unir les connaissances du monde souterrain à celles des grandes étendues septentrionales, faisant de l'endurance, de l'habileté artisanale et de la solidarité familiale les fondements de sa prospérité.

Les descendants de Sinuphel

Les origines des Umli appartiennent aux traditions les plus anciennes du Grand Nord. Les récits conservés par leurs familles mêlent les souvenirs de migrations lointaines, les généalogies des premiers ancêtres et les événements extraordinaires qui auraient donné naissance à leur peuple. Selon l'histoire rapportée dans les développements de MERP, les Umli descendraient de Sinuphel, épouse de Cintapher de Hildórien, qui aurait donné naissance à deux enfants jumeaux, Ucin et Ulaphel. Leur apparence inhabituelle provoqua l'inquiétude et le rejet parmi les Hommes de leur communauté, conduisant leur mère à quitter sa terre natale pour rechercher un lieu où ses enfants pourraient grandir à l'abri des persécutions. Elle entreprit alors un long voyage vers le Nord, traversant des territoires de plus en plus froids avant de trouver refuge dans les régions qui devaient recevoir plus tard le nom d'Ûrd. Cette migration occupe une place centrale dans les traditions umli, car elle rappelle le courage d'une mère qui préféra affronter les dangers des terres inconnues plutôt que d'abandonner ses enfants.

Sinuphel aurait élevé les jumeaux parmi les forêts septentrionales et les montagnes, leur apprenant à reconnaître les ressources disponibles, à construire des abris et à supporter les longues périodes pendant lesquelles la neige rendait les déplacements difficiles. Les récits insistent sur les connaissances qu'elle leur transmit, particulièrement celles qui permettaient de trouver de la nourriture et de conserver les provisions nécessaires à la survie. Leur existence fut cependant bouleversée lorsqu'un Dragon froid nommé Lamthanc attaqua leur demeure et tua Sinuphel. La disparition de leur mère devint l'événement fondateur de nombreuses traditions familiales, dont certaines conservent encore les descriptions des lieux où elle aurait vécu et les noms des passages empruntés par ses enfants après sa mort. Ucin aurait alors juré de venger Sinuphel et entrepris de poursuivre le Ver jusqu'aux Montagnes de Fer, où il parvint finalement à le chasser de son repaire.

Les traditions qui racontent cet affrontement accordent autant d'importance à la prudence d'Ucin qu'à sa bravoure. Le héros connaissait les dangers des montagnes, savait reconnaître les passages praticables et comprenait qu'un adversaire aussi redoutable ne pouvait être affronté sans préparation. Il aurait étudié les accès du repaire, recherché les moyens de s'y introduire et choisi les circonstances les plus favorables pour déloger le Dragon. La possession de cette demeure marqua une nouvelle étape dans son histoire, puisqu'elle lui permit d'établir un foyer protégé et d'entreprendre les travaux qui devaient assurer la sécurité des générations suivantes. Dans certaines versions du récit, l'ancien repaire de Lamthanc devient ainsi le premier établissement véritablement associé aux ancêtres des Umli, dont les descendants conserveront longtemps le souvenir.

Ucin aurait ensuite épousé une Naine, tandis que sa sœur Ulaphel s'unit à un chasseur du peuple des Lossoth. Leurs descendants auraient conservé certains caractères de leurs parents et formé progressivement des communautés possédant les qualités aujourd'hui associées aux Umli. Cette double union explique la place qu'occupent les Khazâd et les Hommes du Nord dans la mémoire de leur peuple, ainsi que le nom de Demi-Nains employé par certains étrangers. Elle donne également une signification particulière aux deux branches de leur ascendance légendaire : Ucin rappelle les traditions de la pierre et des établissements protégés, tandis qu'Ulaphel demeure associée aux connaissances des chasseurs, aux déplacements dans les régions glacées et aux alliances avec les populations humaines.

Ce récit appartient cependant aux développements propres à MERP, particulièrement à ceux consacrés aux terres septentrionales. Tolkien ne décrit aucune population issue d'unions entre les Hommes et les Nains, et la généalogie de Sinuphel, d'Ucin et d'Ulaphel ne peut donc être considérée comme un événement établi dans ses écrits. Elle constitue une tradition fondatrice de l'univers de jeu, que le Meneur peut interpréter comme une véritable origine légendaire, comme le souvenir transformé d'alliances anciennes ou comme une histoire destinée à expliquer les caractéristiques d'un peuple dont les premiers siècles demeurent obscurs.
